items.title: Z.ai releases GLM-5.4, its first loop transformer model using weight-shared layers for deeper networks without increasing parameters [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Chinese AI lab Z.ai has launched GLM-5.4, its first model employing a loop transformer architecture where a group of weight-shared layers iteratively refines hidden states to deepen the network without adding parameters. This approach follows a similar recent development by Thinking Machines Lab with their Inkling 2 Mini model. GLM-5.4 is currently accessible only via Z.ai's Coding Plan subscription API, which shares an OpenAI-compatible interface with the regular API. Early tests show that GLM-5.4 produces output quality comparable to its predecessor GLM-5.3 and similar to models from OpenAI and Anthropic, marking a stylistic shift from earlier GLM versions. Community plugins are being updated to support the new model as it gains adoption.

items.title: Dario Amodei warns at Congress that open-source AI models pose risks by removing control and oversight [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Dario Amodei testified before Congress expressing concerns that open-source AI models could lead to dangerous outcomes because once models are released openly, the ability to monitor usage, restrict access, and enforce safety measures is lost. He argued that keeping models proprietary allows for control mechanisms such as user monitoring and the ability to disable access, which are not possible with open-source distribution.

items.title: Researchers introduce Distributionally-Verifiable Rewards to improve demographic fidelity in human-behavior simulation by large language models, reducing distributional divergence on OpinionQA dataset [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers propose Distributionally-Verifiable Rewards (DVR), a reinforcement learning approach designed to align large language model-generated survey responses with human demographic distributions. DVR aims to balance individual response accuracy with population-level distributional fidelity, addressing limitations of prior methods that either focus on exact matches or ignore demographic variation. Evaluated on the OpinionQA dataset, DVR reduced Jensen-Shannon divergence by 34.5% in-distribution and 14.6% on held-out questions compared to accuracy-only rewards, while maintaining per-response accuracy. The study highlights that low distributional divergence alone is insufficient to ensure demographic fidelity, emphasizing the need to jointly evaluate accuracy, distributional fit, and demographic structure in human-behavior simulation models.

items.title: Researchers introduce TradeoffBench to expose silent value completion failures in multi-criterion LLM evaluation, finding frequent unsupported winner selections and proposing identified-first evaluation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers identify a common issue in large language model (LLM) evaluation where multi-criterion judges issue strict verdicts without specifying trade-off premises, a problem termed silent value completion. They introduce TradeoffBench, a benchmark that separates rule execution from response scoring, revealing that non-reasoning judges often select unsupported winners in 9% to 81% of conflicts despite passing dominance and equality controls. Reasoning-enabled judges reduce violations but still struggle with omitted trade-offs and divergent scoring. The study analyzes GPT-6.1-sol and other reasoning judges on datasets with unspecified or explicit trade-offs, finding that many strict verdicts omit necessary completion premises. Human-score audits show that averaging peer scores increases disagreement significantly, and declared partial trade-offs improve coverage but introduce some disagreement. The authors conclude that reliable LLM judging requires separate auditing, specification support, explicit trade-offs, and human target agreement to ensure consistent and justified evaluations.

items.title: Researchers introduce Population-Based Post-Training to improve large language model tuning by training multiple models in parallel with dynamic hyperparameter adjustment [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Researchers propose Population-Based Post-Training (PBPT) as a new method for tuning large language models, which trains several models simultaneously and adjusts hyperparameters dynamically through population-based training. PBPT evaluates models periodically, duplicates high performers with perturbed hyperparameters, and replaces low performers, enabling automatic discovery of better training settings. PBPT outperforms compute-matched groups of independent reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) learners on reasoning benchmarks like Enigmata and Nemotron, as well as interactive tool-use environments such as Gaia2 and AppWorld. The approach also recovers from poor initial hyperparameters, improving model performance over the course of training.

items.title: Researchers introduce KernelShift, a benchmarking pipeline to evaluate AI coding agents optimizing CPU kernels across evolving Arm architectural extensions including Neon, SVE, SVE2, and SME2 [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: KernelShift is a new benchmarking framework designed to assess how effectively AI coding agents optimize CPU kernels as hardware architectures evolve, focusing on Arm's specialized extensions. The pipeline converts real-world code repositories into benchmark instances and provides environments for agents to optimize code with direct hardware feedback. The study includes 99 kernels from active projects like ncnn and KleidiAI, covering inference workloads from real model executions. Evaluations show that AI agents outperform auto-vectorized compilers by 2.4 to 19.8 times and exceed general-purpose libraries such as ncnn by up to 2.74 times on established extensions, though they lag behind hand-tuned kernels like KleidiAI. In end-to-end inference of two large language models, agent-generated kernels achieve a 1.3 to 1.6 times speedup over existing fast paths. However, current agents struggle to adapt reliably to newer extensions requiring unfamiliar programming models, such as SME2's matrix tiles.

items.title: Researchers predict which loopholes large language model judges will exploit before reinforcement learning training using exposure and false-positive rates [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers studied how policies trained against large language model (LLM) judges can exploit loopholes in the judges' evaluation criteria. They found that the first loophole a policy exploits can be predicted before reinforcement learning (RL) training by measuring each pattern's exposure, defined as the product of the policy's tendency to produce it and the judge's false-positive rate. This prediction held across multiple experiments involving different judges and seeding patterns into fine-tuning data. The study involved 36 runs with seven judges using a method called GRPO, where patterns were seeded at varying doses in a Latin square design. Results showed that the first exploited loophole consistently had the highest exposure, even when false-positive rates alone did not predict exploitation. Exploitation occurred mainly on difficult prompts where exploiting a loophole provided a significant advantage. The findings suggest that auditing exposure before RL training can identify which loopholes a policy is likely to exploit first, aiding in the design of more robust LLM judges.

items.title: Researchers introduce CivilTime-Bench to evaluate large language models' civil-time reasoning, revealing varied accuracy and generalization challenges across seven models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers have developed CivilTime-Bench, a benchmark designed to test large language models' ability to reason about civil time, including complexities like daylight saving transitions, non-hour offsets, date-line crossings, and ISO week boundaries. They evaluated seven models using over 60,000 training and 10,000 evaluation examples, finding significant variation in zero-shot exact match accuracy and mixed results from contract-aware prompting and few-shot learning. Fine-tuning improved performance on synthetic data with exact match scores between 74.6% and 86.6%, but models struggled to generalize to human-generated data, achieving only 36.6% to 45.2% accuracy. The benchmark and code have been released to facilitate further research in this area.

items.title: Researchers audit SWE-Gym coding tasks, find 74% of unsolved tasks have mislabelled tests rejecting correct fixes, and release SWE-Gym-Verified with 1,087 audited tasks and audit pipeline [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers conducted a systematic audit of SWE-Gym, a reinforcement learning environment for training coding agents, focusing on the correctness of reward labels determined by hidden tests. They found that 74% of tasks never solved by a 9B parameter model contained false negatives where tests rejected correct fixes, compared to 20% for sometimes solved tasks. After repairing or removing mislabelled tasks, models trained on the audited set scored 2.4 to 2.7 points higher on held-out benchmarks than those trained on the original tasks, while simply dropping unsolved tasks did not improve performance. The study also identified that about a quarter of passing patches were false positives, but adding new tests to catch some of these did not significantly affect evaluation scores. The researchers emphasize that pass rates indicate whether a task yields reward but do not guarantee the reward's correctness, highlighting the need to verify reward labels. To support further research, they released SWE-Gym-Verified, which includes 1,087 audited tasks with execution evidence, training sets, and the full audit pipeline.

items.title: Researchers propose Test-Time Recursive Self-Improvement to enhance large language models by iteratively refining answers and updating model weights, improving accuracy by nearly 14% [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Researchers introduce Test-Time Recursive Self-Improvement (TT-RSI), a framework for large language models (LLMs) that improves performance after deployment without labeled data. TT-RSI combines In-Context RSI, which re-solves questions using previous solutions as references, and In-Weight RSI, which distills refinements into the model's weights to surpass initial majority errors and approach an infinite-step refinement limit. Experiments demonstrate that TT-RSI increases average accuracy by 13.89% over the base model and outperforms the strongest self-consistency-based method by 4.79% under the same test-time computational budget, suggesting a promising approach for ongoing LLM improvement during inference.

items.title: Researchers introduce SMB Bench to evaluate language model agents on acting with delayed consequences in multi-day wholesale operations [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers present SMB Bench, a 90-day wholesale simulator with 18 causally paired tasks and an 859-run dataset, to study how language model agents recognize and act on delayed effects of decisions in ongoing business operations. They found that while some models diagnose problems, few change behavior effectively to improve outcomes, highlighting the distinction between diagnosis, action, and business improvement. Using the open model Qwen3.8-27B, the team trained policies on archived business records to better follow customer-protection commitments and reduce severe losses in unseen test scenarios, though profit gains were uncertain. The study reveals challenges in coordinating decisions over time, as early stocking habits affected reliance on emergency supplies and supplier quality, and connects these insights to a learning method that reuses past decisions and outcomes as training experience.

items.title: Study shows feedback-driven prompt refinement improves affective agreement and Bloom's taxonomy classification in educational AI without executor parameter updates [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: This study demonstrates that a shared prompt-refinement method guided by affective and cognitive feedback can enhance agreement with held-out references, improve multi-label classification, and reduce variability in affective generation for educational AI systems without updating executor parameters. The approach was tested using a secondary language model that revised prompts based on discrepancies in affective references and Bloom's taxonomy labels across multiple dialogues and learning outcomes. Results showed reductions in affective error and generation variability alongside significant improvements in classification accuracy, suggesting prompt refinement as a promising technique for adaptive technical instruction, though its impact on workforce learning remains to be evaluated.

items.title: Researchers propose INSEP defense to reduce refusal-direction separability in large language models, mitigating abliteration attacks across eight models from 1B to 14B parameters [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: INSEP is a new defense against abliteration, a white-box attack that induces harmful behavior in large language models by projecting out a refusal direction in activation space. The method fine-tunes models to reduce the separability between harmful and benign activations along this direction, weakening the attack's signal while preserving the model's refusal behavior and response quality. The approach uses adversarial eigendecomposition to identify the most separable prompt subsets and applies a low-rank adapter to reduce their separation. INSEP was benchmarked against six existing defenses under five attacks across eight models from various families, showing top performance on a composite score measuring harm, coherence, directness, over-refusal, and knowledge benchmarks, while maintaining utility. This evaluation represents the largest reported study of abliteration defenses to date.

items.title: Researchers demonstrate an AI agent that writes new capabilities into pretrained language model weights without backpropagation, improving BIG-Bench Hard scores on Qwen2.5 and Gemma-3 models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Researchers show that an AI agent can enhance pretrained language models by adding gated attention heads and MLP neurons within existing layers without using backpropagation or fitting weights to task answers. This method, limited to 50 model passes and without exposure to validation or test data, significantly improves BIG-Bench Hard (BBH) scores for Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct and Gemma-3-1B-it models while maintaining unchanged next-token distributions and identical performance on other benchmarks. The agent also successfully writes exact multiplication capabilities up to 20 digits, outperforming comparable LoRA methods. The experiments were rigorously controlled with sealed test sets and timestamped manifests, and evaluations confirmed success across multiple subtasks and tests. Some modules showed minor side effects, and a few sessions reached the 12-hour runtime limit without completing a module, indicating areas for further refinement.

items.title: Researchers propose DoC framework for early, accurate, and stable conversational diagnosis prediction using defer/commit learning with reinforcement training [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers introduce DoC, a two-phase framework designed to improve conversational diagnosis prediction by learning when to defer or commit decisions during clinical dialogues. The approach uses iterative commitment-boundary estimation to generate supervision without annotated commitment times, followed by defer-aware supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning to optimize timeliness, accuracy, and stability. Evaluated on EMSDialog and MediTOD datasets, DoC achieves the highest first-commit accuracy among post-trained methods (76.7% and 51.2%) and the lowest post-commit error rates (16.4% and 48.3%), demonstrating its effectiveness in making early and reliable diagnostic predictions from ongoing conversations.

items.title: VeriLogic introduces reinforcement learning on verifiable logical reasoning traces, improving reasoning accuracy by decomposing and verifying intermediate steps [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: VeriLogic presents a reinforcement learning framework that treats logical reasoning as a sequence of verifiable intermediate steps rather than a single outcome, enabling process-level verification and targeted learning. The approach organizes reasoning into a "Grounding - Optimization - Refinement" pipeline, which grounds reasoning in explicit states, optimizes policies using verifier feedback, and iteratively refines reasoning based on proof diagnostics. Experiments on six benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvements over strong baselines, with average accuracy gains of 6.39% on Qwen3 and 5.00% on Llama-3.1, highlighting the benefits of making reasoning traces verifiable and learnable beyond final-answer supervision.

items.title: Researchers propose Direct Feedback Policy Optimization, a single-trajectory reinforcement learning method that improves task resolution rates for AI coding agents [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers introduce Direct Feedback Policy Optimization (DFPO), a reinforcement learning algorithm designed for AI coding agents that generate, modify, and validate code through multi-turn interactions. Unlike existing methods relying on sparse terminal rewards or repeated sampling, DFPO trains directly from a single trajectory, enabling better assessment of intermediate decisions' impact on task outcomes. DFPO demonstrates higher task resolution rates compared to Group-Relative Policy Optimization (GSPO) when tested with matched base models and execution environments.

items.title: Researchers introduce GameAnything, an open-source platform that converts multimodal inspirations into playable game extensions with iterative refinement and integrated playtesting [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers present GameAnything, a platform designed to transform diverse multimodal inspirations into playable extensions of existing games through iterative development. The system combines coding agents, an independent playtesting critic, persistent development state, and reusable experience memory to enable continuous refinement of game content. They also introduce GameAnything-Bench, a benchmark covering various reference modalities, game creation goals, and environments, which includes exploratory gameplay testing to evaluate both functional correctness and gameplay quality. Evaluations of nine coding agent configurations show that while agents can adapt reference content, they face challenges in creating playable interactions and precise modifications. The study finds that multimodal references enhance content fidelity and iterative refinement improves outcomes, highlighting both the potential and current limitations of AI-driven inspiration-based game development.

items.title: NoeVera system integrates knowledge and experiments to optimize large language model serving configurations, achieving near-optimal results with fewer simulations [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: NoeVera is an agentic system designed to improve optimization of large language model (LLM) serving by creating a persistent knowledge base from papers, code, benchmarks, and experimental results. It uses decision-aware retrieval and role-specific agents to guide experiments and refine knowledge, reducing the number of simulator calls needed to approach optimal configurations. In tests across four serving scenarios, NoeVera achieved configurations within 5% of the optimum using a median of 6-7 simulator calls, outperforming Bayesian optimization and knowledge-free agents. Its configurations improved throughput by about 30% on A100 GPUs while meeting latency goals. The system also demonstrated lower over-generalization in evidence reuse and scored significantly higher on a held-out benchmark compared to other agents, maintaining advantages even when baselines used NoeVera's prompts.

items.title: Researchers identify latent confidence directions in large reasoning models that predict and steer backtracking behavior during answer proposals [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers studied three 32-billion-parameter reasoning models and found that despite reaching correct answers, models often backtrack and propose multiple answers, leading to long reasoning traces. They hypothesized that models maintain an internal representation of uncertainty and extracted a linear latent confidence direction from verbalized confidence signals that correlates with backtracking behavior. By steering this latent confidence direction, the researchers modulated the length of response traces and the number of answer proposals with minimal impact on accuracy. Applying this approach from the start of generation also shortened traces and influenced the linguistic confidence of proposals. The study reveals a close relationship between a model's internal confidence representation and its tendency to backtrack or commit to answers during reasoning.

items.title: Which Failure Does an Intervention Repair? When Agent Interventions Help, and Where Self-Evolving Skills Stall [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2611.29290v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: An intervention that improves one agent can break another, and adding a stronger harness on top need not repair the damage. Agent interventions such as skills, harnesses, and extra inference budget are nonetheless usually credited with one average gain, measured under one setup. We ask instead when each intervention helps and which failure it repairs. A matched factorial study over nine benchmarks, four models, four skill conditions, four harness levels, and three budgets, with nearly 0.9 million trajectories, changes one axis at a time. No configuration is best everywhere, interventions interact rather than add, and a harness can absorb a skill's gain, rescue a failure the skill causes, or leave the gain intact. The failure left by the current system points to the fix: missing knowledge to a stronger model, execution errors to a richer harness. Yet feedback is not recovery: a matched recovery repairs mainly failures that leave a visible error signal. Skills that evolve from the agent's own experience hit a bottleneck: they rarely beat a short human-written skill, can learn dataset shortcuts, break when moved to another model, and cannot supply missing facts, which outside information does. A benchmark-level switch to the model favored by a 20-task labeled pilot achieves both higher performance and lower cost than always using the stronger model. Agent interventions should be judged by which failure they repair and under which configuration.

items.title: SAE-Audit: Clinical-Trial Prediction via Inference-Time Optimization of Black-Box LLMs Audited by Sparse Autoencoder Evidence [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2611.29368v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Clinical trials are costly and often take years to complete, making early outcome prediction valuable for trial planning. Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to forecast clinical-trial outcomes, yet their predictions remain unreliable and their rationales may not faithfully reflect the evidence underlying their answers. On tasks such as predicting whether a registered clinical trial will complete or terminate early, frontier LLMs perform only modestly above chance in our experiments. We introduce SAE-Audit, which optimizes a black-box LLM at inference time with evidence obtained from a deployable open model. A frozen sparse autoencoder (SAE) on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct is converted into a vocabulary of clinical concepts. Sparse probes fitted on past trials determine which concepts are associated with the outcome. For a new protocol, the concepts detected by the probe are written as evidence, each with the direction and strength of its association with the outcome, and the LLM being audited optimizes its answer in the light of this evidence. Without additional training, SAE-Audit raises balanced accuracy of deepseek-v4-flash by 9.6--12.0 points on five clinical-trial prediction tasks and raises GPT-5.6-terra by 8.0 points on trial completion, exceeding other agentic inference-time optimization methods by a large margin. As an auxiliary, SAE probes module within SAE-Audit is itself accurate and auditable, providing natural-language explanations directly derived from verified concept contributions and protocol evidence, without requiring additional LLMs at inference time. SAE-Audit provides verifiable, concept-level evidence for more accurate and auditable clinical-trial prediction. It can also be embedded into biomedical AI agents such as Biomni to optimize their performance.

items.title: Beyond Accuracy: A Diagnostic Benchmark for Hypothesis-Driven Experiment Planning in LLM Agents [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2611.29467v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Evaluating large language model (LLM) agents on scientific tasks typically reduces to final-task accuracy, which obscures where reasoning succeeds or breaks down. We introduce a benchmark and diagnostic evaluation framework for hypothesis-driven adaptive experimental planning in closed-world system identification, instantiated in kinetic mechanism identification. The framework goes beyond final accuracy in two ways. First, we evaluate exploration behavior by quantifying the extent to which agents exhibit space-filling or corner-seeking patterns in the experimental design space. Second, we decompose the reasoning process into four interpretable steps: belief update, hypothesis discrimination, discriminative experiment design, and predictive reasoning under interventions, each scored separately on reasoning traces. Across ten LLM agents, we find that stronger agents outperform both adaptive (Bayesian optimization) and non-adaptive (Latin hypercube) baselines and exhibit exploration patterns inconsistent with naive heuristics. Decomposing reasoning reveals that the stronger agents score consistently well across all four steps, whereas weaker agents often succeed at belief update and hypothesis discrimination but are less reliable at translating them into actionable designs and sharp contrastive predictions. Independent expert annotations support predictive reasoning under our stated validation criteria, while evidence for discriminative experiment design is positive but less consistent. The results suggest a gap between recognizing plausible hypotheses and translating them into contrastive predictions, with more tentative evidence for a corresponding experiment-design bottleneck. The benchmark website is available at https://schwallergroup.github.io/beyond-accuracy/.

items.title: Recursive Self-Editing: LLMs Program Their Own Weight Edits for Self-Improvement [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2611.29513v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recursive self-improvement asks a system to improve the very system that improves it. Today's language models improve themselves through data, training recipes or scaffolds. Whenever their weights change, gradient descent writes the update, not the model. We let the model write its own weights. In SELFWRITE, each generation the current model studies its own reasoning on fresh training problems, inspects its own weights and activations in a persistent Python session, and writes a program that constructs a low-rank weight edit for itself from white-box primitives (singular directions, activation contrasts between its right and wrong answers, rank-one projections, tensor computations), with no training or gradient tool. Every candidate is graded once on a hidden gate set against the current model; the best strictly improving edit is merged into the weights, and the edited model writes the next edit. On Qwen3.8-27B and math problems from DAPO-Math, five generations of SELFWRITE raise gate accuracy from 73.95% to 76.45% and accuracy on a held-out test split that the loop never sees from 76.30% to 77.75% (avg@4) and from 82.60% to 84.80% (pass@4), without a single gradient step. A language model can author useful changes to its own weights without gradients, and the edited model keeps writing useful edits.

items.title: Adaptation or Poisoning? Security Risks of Conversational Test-Time Learning in Large Language Models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2611.29532v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Test-time learning (TTL) enables large language models to adapt to unlabeled inputs during deployment. The model updates a lightweight adapter by minimizing the next-token prediction loss on the input it receives. When these updates persist across conversation turns, every user query serves both as the request answered in the current turn and as adaptation data for later turns. By choosing the queries used for adaptation, an attacker can influence parameter updates and weaken safety alignment through ordinary interactions with a TTL chat service. To demonstrate this risk, we introduce Progressive Test-Time Adaptation Poisoning (P-TAP), a query-only multi-turn attack that jailbreaks the model by poisoning its session adapter through the service's own updates. A sequence of escalating adversarial queries shapes the adapter turn by turn; the final harmful request is then answered under the accumulated state without itself being used for adaptation. Across four open-weight instruction-tuned models, enabling updates raises attack success rates on average by 13.00 percentage points under greedy decoding and by 22.25 points under best-of-10 sampling, relative to matched sessions receiving the same queries without updates. Answering adversarial queries but adapting on unrelated text or on benign text about the same topic removes most of this increase. Among existing safeguards, screening incoming queries flags every attack stream before the final request, while a perplexity-based detector of unsafe adaptation flags none of the successful attacks.

items.title: SAEPO: Sparse-Autoencoder-Guided Credit Assignment for Policy Optimization [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2611.29936v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) has demonstrated strong performance in improving large language model (LLM) reasoning, yet its credit-assignment signal remains coarse. Outcome verifiers provide scalable supervision by judging whether a completed response is correct, but they do not directly indicate which intermediate reasoning tokens contribute to success or failure. As a result, policy optimization can be inefficient, especially when training base models directly from sparse outcome feedback. In this paper, we introduce SAEPO, a Sparse AutoEncoder-guided token-level credit assignment method for outcome-supervised Policy Optimization. Rather than treating correctness only as a rollout-level (sequence-level) signal, SAEPO uses a pretrained sparse autoencoder (SAE) to build token-level semantic representations within reasoning trajectories; it scores each token based on the SAE concepts (e.g., penalizing wrong "final-answer" tokens but rewarding correct "reasoning-process" tokens), learned in an unsupervised manner, to achieve fine-grained credit assignment. SAEPO is a plug-in advantage-shaping module compatible with various policy optimization algorithms. We instantiate SAEPO with both GRPO and GSPO, covering token-ratio and sequence-ratio policy-gradient objectives, and evaluate SAEPO across three LLM backbones on six math and two code benchmarks. Empirical results show that SAEPO improves both the math and code benchmark averages over the matched baselines, with gains of up to 6.63% and 5.57%, respectively. On Qwen3-1.7B-Base, training curves also show faster early accuracy growth. Feature and token-level analyses suggest that the SAE-derived signal favors question-relevant concepts and reasoning tokens.

items.title: Yggdrasil: Tree-Routed Recurrent Experts for State Tracking and Fast CPU Inference [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2611.29954v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Parallel-trainable recurrences such as Mamba, linear attention, and DeltaNet offer constant-cost streaming inference, but they suffer from two limitations: 1) they struggle to track discrete state, and 2) they read every parameter at every step, tying model capacity directly to CPU latency. We introduce Yggdrasil, a recurrent architecture that decouples capacity from per-step compute by looking up each layer's transition in a large, tree-routed bank of recurrent experts. Each router addresses its bank using the current token and the state of the layer below. We prove that this cross-layer context is necessary---a single token-indexed layer of non-expanding transitions with finitely many reachable states cannot perform conditional resets---while avoiding feedback from the layer's own past preserves parallel-scan training. Because each step traverses one tree path and reads a single expert per layer, active weights stay within a few hundred kilobytes in CPU L2 cache while the full bank resides in RAM. Among the parallel-trainable models we evaluate, Yggdrasil is the only one to solve all five state-tracking tasks. At matched active parameter counts, it achieves the lowest test bits on enwik8 (1.540 bpb) and the human genome hg38 (1.567 bpb), while stepping $3.0\times$ and $3.3\times$ faster on a single CPU core ($6.7\,\mu\mathrm{s}$ and $5.8\,\mu\mathrm{s}$) than the fastest streaming baseline, and delivering the highest GPU throughput of all models at batch 1024. On the Genomic Benchmarks, it is the strongest causal model at matched active parameters (86.0% mean accuracy).

items.title: Uncovering the Tells: Efficient Black-Box Audits for LLM Data Contamination [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2611.30639v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Existing methods for assessing training data contamination in Large Language Models achieve high accuracy, but fundamentally rely on gray-box access, rendering them inapplicable to fully black-box environments. This limitation forces auditors to rely on full-sequence sampling or rigid heuristics, both of which incur prohibitive inference costs and struggle to isolate the underlying memorization signal. To overcome this, we propose a generation-based black-box framework that infers context-induced information gain from targeted token discrepancies. We introduce a budget-constrained auditing regime, building on the empirical observation that the membership signal is highly sparse and concentrated in a few highly informative tokens. We formalize this sparsity, showing why uniform sampling needs many more samples than a policy that targets informative positions. Empirically, our approach achieves state-of-the-art black-box separation accuracy while needing about 3x fewer queries than uniform position sampling. Finally, we apply this methodology to closed frontier models, exploring its capacity and limits in surfacing potential training data overlaps on commercial APIs.

items.title: Can Latent Reasoning Drive LLM Outputs Without a Trace? [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2611.31015v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLMs typically solve complex tasks with chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning, which is also the main tool for monitoring them for misaligned behavior. However, standard transformers can also solve tasks with complete latent reasoning (CLR), carrying out the whole task internally and outputting only the final answer. Theory bounds the depth of CLR, the number of sequential steps it can carry out, and recent work measured it to be shallow. In this work, we ask whether CLR is deep enough for a model to pursue a hidden objective that requires reasoning. Such a model would generate a CoT that appears to solve the given task, while a latent multi-step computation decides its answer based on the hidden objective. First, we show that a simple auxiliary loss allows models to solve a multi-step task latently at least 5x deeper than previously reported. Then, in two common tasks, decision-making and code generation, we train a model to pursue such a hidden objective, which decides a loan or plants a vulnerability. The model's CoT justifies the output with no trace of the hidden objective, and a strong LLM monitor does not flag it. Finally, using activation patching, we find that the latent computation is completed before the model generates its CoT, which takes no part in it. Altogether, we show that a hidden objective that requires reasoning can go unseen by a monitor that reads only the output.

items.title: Attention Temperature Confounds Zero-Shot Context Extension [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2611.31113v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A training-time attention change is usually judged for zero-shot context extension against a dense baseline beyond the training length at the default temperature, $\tau = 1$. The outcome depends on how miscalibrated the baseline is there: the share of perplexity it recovers when its logits are sharpened by one scalar. Under the standard recipe (fp32 master weights), an 8k-trained baseline is 8-15% miscalibrated at 30k in three seed-paired 365M twins; in one of them this makes the block-sparse-trained twin look 7% better, which calibration removes. In pure-bf16 training without master weights the miscalibration is several times larger: an AdamW step ($\beta_2 = 0.95$) on a gain initialised at 1.0 is below half the bf16 spacing at peak learning rates under $1.7\times10^{-3}$, so gains never move (22 checkpoints), the baseline is 37-58% miscalibrated, and block-sparse pretraining, attention dropout and ALiBi look 6-35% better. Calibrating one temperature per model and length removes all three advantages, leaves ALiBi 5% behind RoPE and keeps part of the gain of a positive control, NTK-aware scaling. Unfreezing the gains reverses the block-sparse advantage at 365M and removes 71-89% of it at 1.2B. We recommend reporting extension results at calibrated temperatures and checking that normalisation gains moved.

items.title: Token Noise and the Illusion of Preference: A Shapley Value Framework for Auditing LLM-Simulated Choice Experiments [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2404.01332v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large language models are increasingly used to simulate human respondents in choice experiments, yet their answers depend on the exact tokens of a prompt rather than on the offered products alone. I show that invisible characters, blank lines, or minor wording changes shift or reverse simulated choice probabilities. This sensitivity, which I term token noise, creates an illusion of preference and exposes studies to prompt hacking. I introduce a Shapley value audit that divides a model's choice response among the pieces of its prompt and reads each share beside the effect of removing that piece. The edit game divides the effect of several wording and formatting changes beside an actual price change. The word game divides a prompt's response across its words or tokens and summarizes the credit earned by the product attributes as the attribute share. Across four open-weight models and three product categories, wording and formatting edits could rival a substantive price change, while product attributes consistently received a minority of the word-level credit, sometimes less than the answer instruction. Framing cues could take credit from the very price they emphasized and frequently vanished or reversed across equivalent wordings of the question. A persona (even a bare statement that the respondent is a consumer) also shifted choice probabilities and the attributes' credit. Declared with its "players," reference, scale, and uncertainty, my audit separates what a simulated respondent prefers from how the question was asked, the distinction a study must draw before it reads a simulated choice as a preference.

items.title: JustLogic: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Evaluating Deductive Reasoning in Large Language Models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2501.14851v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Logical reasoning is a critical component of Large Language Models (LLMs), and substantial research efforts in recent years have aimed to enhance their deductive reasoning abilities. However, existing deductive reasoning benchmarks suffer from significant constraints that restrict their utility, i.e., the lack of task complexity, the presence of prior knowledge as a confounder, and superficial error analysis. To address these deficiencies, we introduce JustLogic, a synthetically generated benchmark for evaluating deduction in propositional logic. Within this fragment, JustLogic is (i) complex, capable of generating a diverse range of linguistic patterns, vocabulary, and argument structures, (ii) prior knowledge independent, substantially reducing the advantage of models possessing prior knowledge so that questions are answerable from the given premises alone, and (iii) capable of in-depth error analysis on the heterogeneous effects of proof size and argument form on model accuracy. Our experimental results on JustLogic reveal that (i) several state-of-the-art (SOTA) reasoning LLMs score above the human average on JustLogic, although only DeepSeek R1's margin is significant on the matched items after correction for multiple comparisons, and (ii) the evaluated non-reasoning models score below the human average. Given the small human study (18 participants, seven questions each), these comparisons are indicative. All code and data are available at https://github.com/michaelchen-lab/JustLogic

items.title: When Chain-of-Thought Fails, the Solution Hides in the Hidden States [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2604.23351v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Whether intermediate reasoning is computationally useful or merely explanatory depends on whether chain-of-thought (CoT) tokens contain task-solving information. We present a mechanistic causal analysis of CoT on GSM8K using activation patching: transferring token-level hidden states from an arithmetic CoT generation to a direct-answer run for the same question, then measuring the effect on final-answer accuracy. Across models, patching can elicit generations that lead to correct answers, revealing that individual CoT hidden states can encode sufficient task-solving information even when the original CoT trace is incorrect. This information is more prevalent in correct than incorrect CoT runs and is unevenly distributed across tokens, concentrating in mid-to-late layers and appearing earlier in the reasoning trace. Moreover, patching from language tokens such as verbs and entities more frequently elicits correct reasoning traces, whereas patches from mathematical tokens more often produce answer-proximal generations that rarely succeed. Further analysis shows that earlier CoT tokens concentrate recoverable information, while later ones require broader search to find the correct answer. Together, these findings show that CoT encodes recoverable, token-level task-solving information, revealing how arithmetic reasoning is represented, accessed, and disrupted.

items.title: Post-training is (Massive) Supervised Learning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2606.07527v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The prevailing paradigm for training LLMs has evolved to rely on a massive post-training phase consisting of SFT and RL. In this position paper, we argue that this methodology effectively marks a reversion to the ``pre-train then fine-tune'' approach of the BERT era, explicitly tailoring models to the desired behaviors and specific benchmarks on which they are evaluated. We begin with a historical overview of LLMs, describing the different phases of the LLM evolution. We argue that the current landscape is remarkably similar to the early days of LLMs, where task performance heavily relied on fitting the models to in-distribution datasets. To empirically demonstrate this, we compare pre-trained models to randomly initialized ones, by fine-tuning both variants on modern reasoning datasets and evaluating them on competitive math and code benchmarks. We show that models post-trained from scratch yield highly non-trivial performance. Our findings suggest that current post-training methodologies function primarily as a distribution-fitting mechanism. We finish by positing that developing generally capable models and systems requires moving beyond extensive post-training for predefined behaviors, shifting instead toward training procedures where models ``learn how to learn''.

items.title: FOCUS & RePAIR: Mitigating Text Degeneration via Token-Level Guidance for Pruned Large Language Models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2608.26676v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Pruning is a practical approach to compress large language models (LLMs), but it can amplify text degeneration, especially repetition loops, even when perplexity and task accuracy remain largely unchanged. In this work, we present a token-level analysis of this failure mode by viewing decoding as a dynamical process that enters and persists in a small set of recurrent contexts. Our analysis decomposes degeneration into loop entry risk and loop persistence, and shows that persistence is controlled by the escape mass assigned to plausible alternatives within the token sampling set. Motivated by these findings, we propose two token-level guidance objectives for post-pruning fine-tuning. FOCUS reweights distillation toward high-confidence teacher regions to suppress leakage, while RePAIR uses onset-centered positive/negative continuation pairs with a margin loss to promote plausible alternatives and prevent early commitment to repetition loops. Experiments on open-ended continuation and instruction-based generation show that both methods consistently reduce repetition and improve generation quality.

items.title: Sparse Readout Prism: Explaining Logit-Lens Scores in Features Instead of Tokens
items.content_text: arXiv:2609.01936v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Lens methods interpret intermediate hidden states by transporting them to the final layer and decoding them through the unembedding matrix into token scores. Fitted lenses learn their transport map from a training corpus. We find that changing only the corpus can change token rankings for the same hidden state; we call this corpus conditionality. To test whether two differently fitted lenses share unembedding features, we introduce Sparse Readout Prism (SRP), which learns these features by reconstructing each unembedding row as a sparse combination of them. SRP measures each feature's contribution to a lens score without changing the lens's transport. Across six models, SRP reconstructs logit differences more accurately than geometric baselines. On Ministral-3-8B, English and Chinese Jacobian lenses disagree on the top token for all prompts at one layer in both comparisons, versus at most 10% for same-language refits at that layer. On Qwen3.5-9B, disagreement reaches 87% between English and German Jacobian lenses and 94% between English and Chinese ridge lenses. At one layer, SRP finds the same dominant feature in the two lenses' top-token scores for 81% of prompts with English and German Jacobian lenses on Qwen and up to 78% with English and Chinese Jacobian lenses on Ministral.

items.title: Cross-modal RAG: Sub-dimensional Text-to-Image Retrieval-Augmented Generation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2505.21956v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Text-to-image generation increasingly demands access to domain-specific, fine-grained, and rapidly evolving knowledge that pretrained models cannot fully capture, necessitating the integration of retrieval methods. Existing Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) methods attempt to address this by retrieving globally relevant images, but they fail when no single image contains all desired elements from a complex user query. We propose Cross-modal RAG, a novel framework that decomposes both queries and images into sub-dimensional components, enabling subquery-aware retrieval and generation. Our method introduces a hybrid retrieval strategy, combining a sub-dimensional sparse retriever with a dense retriever, to identify a Pareto-optimal set of images, each contributing complementary aspects of the query. During generation, a multimodal large language model is guided to selectively condition on relevant visual features aligned to specific subqueries for subquery-aware image synthesis. Extensive experiments on MS-COCO, Flickr30K, WikiArt, CUB, and ImageNet-LT demonstrate that Cross-modal RAG significantly outperforms existing baselines in the retrieval and further contributes to generation quality, while maintaining high efficiency.

items.title: HyperCLOVA X 8B Omni [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2601.01792v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In this report, we present HyperCLOVA X 8B Omni, the first any-to-any omnimodal model in the HyperCLOVA X family that supports text, audio, and vision as both inputs and outputs. By consolidating multimodal understanding and generation into a single model rather than separate modality-specific pipelines, HyperCLOVA X 8B Omni serves as an 8B-scale omni-pathfinding point toward practical any-to-any omni assistants. At a high level, the model unifies modalities through a shared next-token prediction interface over an interleaved multimodal sequence, while vision and audio encoders inject continuous embeddings for fine-grained understanding and grounding. Empirical evaluations demonstrate competitive performance against comparably sized models across diverse input-output combinations spanning text, audio, and vision, in both Korean and English. We anticipate that the open-weight release of HyperCLOVA X 8B Omni will support a wide range of research and deployment scenarios.

items.title: HyperCLOVA X 32B Think [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2601.03286v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In this report, we present HyperCLOVA X 32B Think, a vision-language model designed with particular emphasis on reasoning within the Korean linguistic and cultural context, as well as agentic ability. HyperCLOVA X 32B Think is pre-trained with a strong focus on reasoning capabilities and subsequently post-trained to support multimodal understanding, enhanced reasoning, agentic behaviors, and alignment with human preferences. Experimental evaluations against comparably sized models demonstrate that our model achieves strong performance on Korean text-to-text and vision-to-text benchmarks, as well as on agent-oriented evaluation tasks. By open-sourcing HyperCLOVA X 32B Think, we aim to support broader adoption and facilitate further research and innovation across both academic and industrial communities.

items.title: Asymptotic Universal Alignment: A New Alignment Framework via Test-Time Scaling [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2601.08777v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Aligning large language models (LLMs) to serve users with heterogeneous and potentially conflicting preferences is a central challenge for personalized and trustworthy AI. We formalize an ideal notion of universal alignment through test-time scaling: for each prompt, the model produces $k\ge 1$ candidate responses and a user selects their preferred one. We introduce $(k,f(k))$-robust alignment, which requires the $k$-output model to have win rate $f(k)$ against any other single-output model, and asymptotic universal alignment (U-alignment), which requires $f(k)\to 1$ as $k\to\infty$. Our main result characterizes the optimal convergence rate: there exists a family of single-output policies whose $k$-sample product policies achieve U-alignment at rate $f(k)=\frac{k}{k+1}$, and no method can achieve a faster rate in general. We show that popular post-training methods, including Nash learning from human feedback (NLHF), can fundamentally underutilize the benefits of test-time scaling. Even though NLHF is optimal for $k=1$, sampling from the resulting (often deterministic) policy cannot guarantee win rates above $\tfrac{1}{2}$ except for an arbitrarily small slack. This stems from a lack of output diversity: existing alignment methods can collapse to a single majority-preferred response, making additional samples redundant. In contrast, our approach preserves output diversity and achieves the optimal test-time scaling rate. In particular, we propose a family of symmetric multi-player alignment games and prove that any symmetric Nash equilibrium policy of the $(k+1)$-player alignment game achieves the optimal $(k,\frac{k}{k+1})$-robust alignment. Finally, we provide theoretical convergence guarantees for self-play learning dynamics in these games and extend the framework to opponents that also generate multiple responses.

items.title: Unsolvability Ceiling in Multi-LLM Routing: An Empirical Study of Evaluation Artifacts [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2605.07395v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Efficient routing across multiple LLMs enables cost-quality tradeoffs by directing queries to the cheapest capable model. Prior work attributes routing headroom to an "unsolvability ceiling", queries no model in the pool can solve. We present a large-scale study of multi-tier LLM routing with 206,000 query-model pairs across six benchmarks (MMLU, MedQA, HumanEval, MBPP, Alpaca, ShareGPT) using the Gemma 4 and Llama 3.1 families. Evaluating with both LLM-as-a-judge and exact-match metrics, we show that a substantial portion of reported unsolvability stems from evaluation artifacts: (i) systematic judge biases favoring verbosity over correctness, (ii) truncation under fixed generation budgets, and (iii) output format mismatches. Through dual-judge validation and exact-match grounding, we reduce measured unsolvability across tasks. We introduce a decomposition framework attributing failures to these artifacts, revealing consistent patterns across domains and model families. These artifacts also distort router training signals: standard routers collapse to majority-class prediction (~79% smallest-tier optimal), confirmed via random-feature and shuffled-label controls, incurring a 13-17 percentage point opportunity cost. We provide actionable recommendations including dual-judge validation, exact-match anchoring, and cost-sensitive objectives. Our findings suggest existing routing headroom estimates are substantially inflated, underscoring the need for reliable evaluation protocols in multi-LLM systems.

items.title: RealICU: Do LLM Agents Understand Long-Context ICU Data? A Benchmark Beyond Behavior Imitation [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2605.13542v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Intensive care units (ICU) generate long, dense and evolving streams of clinical information, where physicians must repeatedly reassess patient states under time pressure, underscoring a clear need for reliable AI decision support. Existing ICU benchmarks typically treat historical clinician actions as ground truth. However, these actions are made under incomplete information and limited temporal context of the underlying patient state, and may therefore be suboptimal, making it difficult to assess the true reasoning capabilities of AI systems. We introduce RealICU, a hindsight-annotated benchmark for evaluating large language models (LLMs) under realistic ICU conditions, where labels are created after senior physicians review the full patient trajectory. We formulate four physician-motivated tasks: assess Patient Status, Acute Problems, Recommended Actions, and Red Flag actions that risk unsafe outcomes. We partition each trajectory with 30-min windows and release two datasets: RealICU-Gold with 930-window annotations from 94 MIMIC-IV patients, and RealICU-Scale with 11,862 windows extended by Oracle, a physician-validated LLM hindsight labeler. Existing LLMs including memory-augmented ones performed poorly on RealICU, exposing two failure modes: a recall-safety tradeoff for clinical recommendations, and an anchoring bias to early interpretations of the patient. We further introduce ICU-Evo to study structured-memory agents that improves long-horizon reasoning but does not fully eliminate safety failures. Together, RealICU provides a clinically grounded testbed for measuring and improving AI sequential decision-support in high-stakes care. Project page: https://chengzhi-leo.github.io/RealICU-Bench/

items.title: To See is Not to Learn: Protecting Multimodal Data from Unauthorized Fine-Tuning of Large Vision-Language Models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2605.14291v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The rapid advancement of Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) is increasingly accompanied by unauthorized scraping and training on multimodal web data, posing copyright and privacy risks to data owners. Existing countermeasures, such as machine unlearning and watermarks, are inherently post-hoc approaches that act only after intellectual property infringement has already occurred. In this work, we propose MMGuard to empower data owners to proactively protect their multimodal data against unauthorized LVLM fine-tuning. MMGuard generates unlearnable examples by injecting human-imperceptible perturbations that exploit the learning dynamics of LVLMs. By minimizing the training loss, the perturbation creates an optimization shortcut, causing the model to overfit to the noise and thereby degrading downstream performance when the perturbation is absent during inference. To further strengthen this defense, MMGuard introduces a cross-modal binding disruption, shifting LVLM attention to enforce a spurious correlation between the noise and the training target with theoretical guarantees. MMGuard is evaluated against nine open-source LVLMs across six datasets. Our results demonstrate effective, stealthy, and robust protection under white-box, gray-box, and no-box threat models, establishing a mechanistic advantage in proactively defending against unauthorized fine-tuning exploitation.

items.title: From Inference to Adaptation: Vision-Language Model Test-Time Adaptation via a Unified Optimal Transport View [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2608.18339v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) have demonstrated remarkable zero-shot capabilities yet remain sensitive to real-world distribution shifts. Although significant efforts are devoted to adapting VLMs at test time, they rely heavily on noisy pseudo-labels predicted from cross-modal embedding similarities during inference, which are unreliable under distribution shifts and mislead the adaptation. Moreover, existing methods largely overlook the critical relational structures across different modalities during test-time adaptation, whose supervision signals remain surprisingly robust under distribution shifts. In this work, we aim to jointly align the cross-modal semantics and intra-modal relational structures across modalities at test time to improve VLM adaptation. At the inference stage, we formulate the zero-shot image classification task as a cross-modal alignment problem via a Fused Gromov-Wasserstein (FGW) formulation, which considers both cross-modal semantics and intra-modal structures to generate robust pseudo-labels. At the adaptation stage, we propose a multi-level InfoNCE loss to leverage both the semantical and relational alignment supervision from the inference stage, empowering fine-grained adaptation of VLMs under distribution shifts with additional structural consistency. Finally, we bridge the inference and adaptation stages of our method by proving a mathematical equivalence between their objective functions, thereby revealing the mutual benefits of these two stages from a theoretical perspective. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of our methods, outperforming the best-performing methods by up to 3% while maintaining a superior balance between effectiveness and efficiency.

items.title: Surprising Success, Repeated Failure: Entropy-Guided Credit Assignment for Exploration in LLM Reasoning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2609.33781v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) enhances reasoning in large language models (LLMs) through outcome-level feedback, yet recent approaches to finer-grained credit assignment often require auxiliary models, additional sampling, or privileged information. Although policy entropy provides a readily available signal, prioritizing uncertain positions under both reinforcement and penalization concentrates penalties where failed responses still retain alternatives for recovery, which can suppress opportunities for exploration. To address this, we introduce Entropic Advantage Policy Optimization (EAPO), an entropy-guided credit assignment method that treats success and failure asymmetrically. Specifically, motivated by the observation that success under uncertainty is less repeatable while confident failures tend to recur, EAPO couples normalized policy entropy with the sign of the response advantage to reinforce surprising success and correct repeated failure. It assigns stronger reinforcement to high-entropy decisions in successful responses and stronger penalties to low-entropy decisions in failed responses, while attenuating penalties at uncertain positions to preserve opportunities for recovery. By redistributing the response advantage across tokens, EAPO derives token-level credit directly from existing rollout signals without additional supervision. We validate EAPO on a range of reasoning tasks across both base and reasoning backbones, demonstrating that it achieves the best overall performance. We further show that EAPO promotes more effective exploration, broadening problem coverage and diversifying successful reasoning strategies.

items.title: FAER: A Negative-Result Audit of Offline Trajectory Replay Selection on GSM8K [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.00385v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Offline trajectory replay selects model-generated reasoning traces from a frozen cache for supervised fine-tuning (SFT), yet cache-side answer correctness need not predict downstream accuracy on unseen problems. We report a failure-retaining audit of offline response SFT on GSM8K with Qwen3-1.7B fp16 LoRA over a frozen 384-row cache (256 training rows and 128 excluded held-out rows). Across three seeds (13, 17, 23) on a 256-problem test split, all three 32-row replay rules (uniform, format-feedback, and feedback-aware) obtain mean strict accuracies (0.7786, 0.7682, and 0.7956) below the no-update base model (0.8008), and every paired 95% confidence interval spans zero. Selector ranking is post-hoc unidentified (3 completed selectors versus the repaired protocol's minimum of 5, with rank correlation spanning both signs). Under an 8,192-supervised-token windowed schedule, 9 of 12 runs halt under calibration drift or unresolved nonfinite training loss or gradients, leaving only full-cache replay completed at 0.7721. A repaired campaign with dynamic loss scaling halted at its learning-rate pilot under reference-solution loss drift before accessing the 346-problem locked test split. Because the gold-rationale positive control was never executed, these negative results cannot separate cache quality, selector quality, and learner-protocol limits. Our one positive finding separates parser repair from prompt changes on a 64-problem audit split: reparsing fixed base generations with a Decimal extractor raises parse rate from 0.8750 to 1.0000 and accuracy from 0.7344 to 0.8281, whereas appending a format suffix flips 0.2500 of canonical answers. A preregistered replication on 512 fresh GSM8K training problems reproduces this parser-only gain (+8.40 pp, 95% CI [+6.05, +10.94]) for this checkpoint. We contribute a ledger-traceable negative-result record and 9 lessons learned.

items.title: RouteAudit: A Negative Result on Adaptive Multi-Verifier Routing under Matched Fixed-Subset Controls [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.02808v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Apparent savings from adaptive verifier routing can come from a fixed verifier subset. We audit GSM8K using cached Qwen3.5-0.8B or Qwen3.5-2B candidates paired with Qwen3-4B, three LLM verifiers, 1,319 held-out requests, and 5 router seeds. Our shared-fusion audit compares routers with the complete fixed-subset envelope, including zero-call abstention, under matched prices and scoring. Calibration-selected single-call verification matches full static verification in 3 of 4 cells. In a separate comparison using the original fusion rules and two-verifier catalog, archived learned and offline-RL routers lose 0.038 to 0.171 in quality against matched static SF+SA. Across 480 budget-matched offline fits in six router families, the family envelope gain is zero in each cell at the primary price. No locked router obtains a positive simultaneous bootstrap lower bound across 68 cell-by-price points. None is classified as complete-static dominant, and all 4 primary-price points are inconclusive. At the primary price, the tested-family gain upper bound is at most 0.002. The oracle headroom upper bound is 0.034 to 0.045, above our 0.01 margin, leaving meaningful gains open. At 45 of 64 grid points excluding the primary price, the oracle lower bound exceeds 0.01 and the tested-family upper bound is at most 0.01. Coverage of these envelope bounds remains unverified. At a true gain of 0.03, the procedure rejects on 44.1% of points, and planted-effect family coverage ranges from 0.923 to 0.931. We report lessons from this catalog.

items.title: Match the Canvas, Not Just the Answer: Predictability-Aware SFT for Diffusion Language Models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.18001v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Diffusion language models (DLMs) enable flexible parallel generation by resolving tokens according to the model's evolving predictability rather than a fixed left-to-right order. This flexibility, however, introduces training choices absent from standard autoregressive teacher forcing: which reference tokens are visible when a target is supervised and how much generation space is allocated. Standard supervised fine-tuning (SFT) typically makes these choices through random masking, independently of inference. Our analysis shows how this training-inference mismatch can misdirect supervision. Random masking can conceal prediction errors or penalize uncertainty that decoding would otherwise resolve, while the attention-visible input length can change which response formulations the model favors, even when the underlying solution is unchanged. Motivated by these findings, we propose Predictability-Aware Canvas Selection and Supervision (PACS), an SFT method. PACS uses the model's own predictability to select each example's attention-visible input length and supervises reference tokens immediately before their confidence-guided revelation. Across reasoning and code-generation benchmarks, PACS consistently achieves the highest mean accuracy among the compared SFT methods, with gains of up to 12.84 percentage points over vanilla SFT on individual benchmarks. Code will be released upon publication.

items.title: PACE: More Agents, More Samples, or More Thinking? Untangling Coordination, Ensembling, and Test-Time Compute in Multi-Agent LLMs [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2611.17610v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Multi-agent language model evaluations often compare a communicating system with a single greedy pass, which confounds coordination with extra samples and test-time compute. We introduce Parity-Aware Compute Evaluation (PACE): a six-dimensional resource vector, four baseline categories, and a directional rule that credits a gain only against a baseline using at least as much of the declared resources and rules a gain out against any baseline using no more. We audit 9 published studies. Across the 72 deduplicated baseline cells that report both a greedy and a sampled baseline, the sampling gap, by which the sampled baseline lowers the multi-agent difference, averages -0.036 with studies weighted equally (negative in 64 cells), and 53 of the 123 paired contrasts that beat a greedy pass become nonpositive against the sampled baseline. Against sampled or budget-matched baselines the mean difference is -0.042; all eight Category B/C study means are negative and the one Category D study is positive. In a controlled experiment with an open-weight model, debate and mixture-of-agents do not clear the equal-token self-consistency frontier on MMLU-Pro (debate -0.015); on Hidden Profile, split-view debate exceeds a lower-budget pool yet trails content-mismatched placebo and four-choice chance. We release a seven-item checklist, an evaluation card, and command-line utilities.

items.title: SkillBuffBench: Measuring What Agent Skills Contribute across Harnesses, Models, Skill Access Modes and Memory [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2611.22017v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Agent Skills, file-based packages of procedural knowledge that a coding agent can discover and load on demand, are now shipped by every major agent harness, yet the evidence for how much they help comes almost entirely from settings in which the right Skill is hand-picked for the task and the agent starts from a blank slate. Neither holds in deployment, where an agent chooses from whatever library happens to be installed and frequently carries memory from earlier work. We present SkillBuffBench, a benchmark and paired evaluation protocol that treats Skill access as a three-level factor (no Skill, a curated Skill, and automatic invocation from an installed library), crosses it with memory (off and on), with four agent harnesses and with multiple models (the state-of-the-art proprietary models from Anthropic, Google and OpenAI, and the state-of-the-art open-weight models from Chinese providers), every model being run under every harness, and evaluates the result on research tasks contributed by domain experts together with the Skills they use, currently in materials science and biology, with the suite extended on a rolling basis. Every run is marked by a deterministic verifier; uncertainty is reported with a paired, task-level bootstrap; and cost, agent rounds and wall-clock time are reported alongside the score rather than folded into it. This version of the paper describes the design of the benchmark, its evaluation protocol and its current tasks and Skills. The evaluation is in progress: results will be added once the runs are complete, and the task suite, results and analysis will continue to be updated on a rolling basis.

items.title: PaMuk-Bench: A Parallel Multilingual Multitask Benchmark for Vision-Language Tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2611.27521v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: While vision-language models (VLMs) currently obtain notable results for highly-studied languages, e.g. English, they exhibit significant performance drops in certain low-resource languages, especially due to the lack of annotated datasets. To this end, we propose PaMuk-Bench, a novel parallel multilingual multitask benchmark for vision-language tasks. Our benchmark includes a set of over 10K curated English prompts that are translated into six languages: Arabic, Danish, French, Hindi, Italian, Romanian. Parallel translations, which are obtained via a semi-automatic process, along with accompanying generated and retrieved images enable the comparative development and evaluation of VLMs across a wide range of tasks: text-to-image generation, image captioning, content-based image retrieval, image generation difficulty estimation, image retrieval difficulty estimation. We empirically show that zero-shot English and multilingual pre-trained VLMs compare consistently worse than their fine-tuned counterparts, confirming that PaMuk-Bench is a valuable resource that can drastically reduce the language gap across a variety of VLM architectures and tasks. PaMuk-Bench is available at https://github.com/ghesil/pamuk_bench.
